\chapter{What the Ear Cannot Hear}
\label{ch:fr-silent}
\hlchaptermodality{42}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I know why a written consonant at the end of a French word is silent, what the plural and the feminine do about it, and what happens to some after a negative.}

One sound rule and the four spellings that hang off it. The chapter names the thing the reader has been working around since the numbers -- a final consonant is silent -- and then shows the plural, the feminine, the -x plural and the negative partitive as four consequences of it rather than four separate facts.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la consonne finale]{la consonne finale — the rule under half this book}

\label{lesson:FR-C38-consonne-finale}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{quand}, \textbf{et}, \textbf{parlez}, \textbf{des}. Four words, four written consonants at the end, and not one of them sounded. Nobody has yet said why.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the joiner Latin used for \emph{more} — \emph{mais}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
A consonant written at the end of a French word is normally \textbf{not pronounced}.
\end{quote}

\emph{Petit} is \emph{puh-TEE}. \emph{Grand} is \emph{grahn}. \emph{Trois} is \emph{trwah}. \emph{Beaucoup} is \emph{boh-KOO}. The letter is on the page and not in the mouth.

Those letters were once sounded. Old French said the \emph{t} of \emph{petit} and the \emph{s} of \emph{trois}, and over centuries the mouth dropped them while the spelling stayed where it was. Every silent consonant in French is a fossil of a sound the language used to make.

Two things bring them back to life, and you own both:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Liaison.} Before a vowel the consonant wakes up — \emph{des amis} is \emph{day-ZAH-mee}, \emph{quand est-ce que} is \emph{kahn-TESS-kuh}. You met this on the numbers.
  \item \textbf{A following -e.} Add an \emph{-e} and the consonant is no longer final, so it is no longer silent. That is the next lesson.
\end{itemize}

There are exceptions worth naming, and the shortest way to hold them is the word \textbf{CaReFuL} — \emph{c}, \emph{r}, \emph{f}, \emph{l} are the four consonants that usually \textbf{do} sound at the end: \emph{avec}, \emph{bonjour}, \emph{neuf}, \emph{il}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item silent — \textquotedblleft{}petit, grand, trois, beaucoup\textquotedblright{}
  \item woken by a vowel — \textquotedblleft{}des amis\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}quand est-ce que\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four that usually sound — \textquotedblleft{}avec, bonjour, neuf, il\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one \emph{t} that never wakes — \textquotedblleft{}et un café\textquotedblright{}
  \item a silent letter you have been pointing with — \textquotedblleft{}ces cafés\textquotedblright{}, where the \emph{s} is heard only before a vowel
  \item the accent that is not a sound either — \textquotedblleft{}là\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}là-bas\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What happens to a consonant written at the end of a French word? (\textbf{It is normally silent.}) What wakes it? (\textbf{A following vowel} — liaison.) Which four usually sound anyway? (\emph{\textbf{C, r, f, l}} — \emph{careful}.) And which word refuses to make its liaison at all? (\emph{\textbf{Et}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[le plural en -s]{le pluriel en -s — written, and never heard}

\label{lesson:FR-C38-pluriel-s}



\begin{quote}
A final consonant is silent. A plural is written with a final \textbf{s}. Put the two facts together before you read on.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
A French noun takes \textbf{-s} in the plural, and that \textbf{-s} is silent.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{le café $\to$ les cafés} — \emph{luh ka-FAY} $\to$ \emph{lay ka-FAY}
\end{quote}

Say those two aloud and listen. The noun did not change at all. Only the article in front of it did.

That is the whole reason the article system matters so much here. \textbf{le}, \textbf{la}, \textbf{les}, \textbf{un}, \textbf{une}, \textbf{des} are not ornament — they are the \textbf{only} place a French listener can hear that more than one thing is meant. Drop the article, as English does with a bare plural, and a French sentence becomes genuinely ambiguous.

The \textbf{-s} does come back before a vowel, as a \textbf{z}: \emph{les amis} is \emph{lay-ZAH-mee}. So the plural is audible exactly when the next word begins with a vowel and inaudible otherwise, which is one more reason liaison is not optional politeness.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair, listening for no difference — \textquotedblleft{}le café, les cafés\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le chien, les chiens; le chat, les chats\textquotedblright{}
  \item the plural that IS audible — \textquotedblleft{}les amis\textquotedblright{}, \emph{lay-ZAH-mee}
  \item with \emph{des} — \textquotedblleft{}des cafés, des chiens, des œufs\textquotedblright{}
  \item the article carrying the whole load — \textquotedblleft{}le\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}les\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the plural \emph{-s} pronounced? (\textbf{No} — it is a final consonant.) Then what tells a listener a plural is meant? (\textbf{The article} — \emph{les}, \emph{des}.) When does the \emph{-s} come back? (\textbf{Before a vowel}, as a \emph{z}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[petit, petite]{petit, petite — the ending that wakes the letter before it}

\label{lesson:FR-C38-feminin-e}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{bon} and \textbf{bonne}. You have had both since page one, and the difference between them has never been named.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
The feminine of an adjective adds \textbf{-e}. That \textbf{-e} is itself silent — and it makes the consonant in front of it audible.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{petit} — \emph{puh-TEE}. · \textbf{petite} — \emph{puh-TEET}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{grand} — \emph{grahn}. · \textbf{grande} — \emph{grahnd}.
\end{quote}

Nothing is added to the sound at the end. What changes is that the \emph{t} and the \emph{d} stop being final, so the rule from two lessons ago no longer silences them.

This is worth holding on to, because it makes the feminine \textbf{easier to hear than to see}. A French listener knows \emph{petite} from \emph{petit} instantly — one ends in a consonant and one does not — while a reader has to notice a letter that is never said.

The colours behave the same way, and you already own three of them: \emph{vert} is \emph{vair} and \emph{verte} is \emph{vairt}; \emph{blanc} and \emph{blanche}; \emph{noir} and \emph{noire}, where the \emph{r} was already sounding and nothing changes at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair, hearing the \emph{t} arrive — \textquotedblleft{}petit, petite\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}grand, grande\textquotedblright{}
  \item the colours — \textquotedblleft{}vert, verte; blanc, blanche\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that does not change — \textquotedblleft{}noir, noire\textquotedblright{}
  \item with a noun behind it — \textquotedblleft{}le vin blanc\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}la maison blanche\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair you have had since page one — \textquotedblleft{}bon, bonne\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is the feminine \emph{-e} pronounced? (\textbf{No.}) Then what does it do? (\textbf{It stops the consonant before it being final}, so that consonant sounds.) Is the feminine easier to hear or to see? (\textbf{To hear} — the difference is a whole consonant.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[les bateaux]{les bateaux — the plural that is not irregular}

\label{lesson:FR-C38-pluriel-x}



\begin{quote}
You were told that the \emph{u} in \textbf{au} was once an \emph{l}. That fact has been waiting two chapters to pay for itself.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
Nouns ending in \textbf{-eau} and \textbf{-eu} take \textbf{-x} in the plural instead of \textbf{-s}, and nouns already ending in \textbf{-s}, \textbf{-x} or \textbf{-z} take nothing.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{le bateau $\to$ les bateaux} · \textbf{le cheveu $\to$ les cheveux} · \textbf{le fils $\to$ les fils}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{x} is silent, exactly as the \textbf{s} is, so once again the article carries the whole plural.

Two of the three lines are the same story you already have. \textbf{Cheval} became \textbf{chevaux} because \emph{-als} turned into \emph{-aus}, and French wrote that \emph{-aus} as \emph{-aux}. That is the change that made \textbf{au} out of \emph{à} + \emph{le} — an \emph{l} softening into a \emph{u} somewhere around the twelfth century, right across the language.

So \emph{chevaux} is not an irregular plural at all. It is a perfectly regular plural of a word whose \emph{l} melted, and the strange-looking \emph{x} is a spelling convention for a \emph{u-s} that got there honestly.

The third line is simpler still: a word that already ends in \emph{s}, \emph{x} or \emph{z} has nowhere to put another one, so it does not try. \textbf{Le fils} and \textbf{les fils} are the same six letters.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}le bateau, les bateaux\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le cheveu, les cheveux\textquotedblright{}
  \item the invariable — \textquotedblleft{}le fils, les fils\textquotedblright{}
  \item the \emph{l} that melted — \textquotedblleft{}cheval, chevaux\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}à le, au\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the indefinite — \textquotedblleft{}des bateaux, des cheveux\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which endings take \emph{-x}? (\emph{\textbf{-eau}} and \emph{\textbf{-eu}}.) Which take nothing at all? (\textbf{Words already ending in \emph{s}, \emph{x} or \emph{z}}.) Why is \emph{chevaux} not really irregular? (\textbf{Its \emph{l} melted into a \emph{u}}, the same change that made \emph{au}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[pas de pain]{pas de pain — where the partitive collapses}

\label{lesson:FR-C38-pas-de}



\begin{quote}
Say the four shapes of \emph{some}: \textbf{du}, \textbf{de la}, \textbf{de l'}, \textbf{des}. Now negate one of them and watch all four become the same word.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
After a negative, \textbf{du}, \textbf{de la}, \textbf{de l'} and \textbf{des} all become a bare \textbf{de}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{J'ai du pain.} $\to$ \textbf{Je n'ai pas de pain.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Il y a des cafés.} $\to$ \textbf{Il n'y a pas de cafés.}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je bois de l'eau.} $\to$ \textbf{Je ne bois pas d'eau.}
\end{quote}

Four shapes, one replacement, and it elides before a vowel like everything else.

The reason is in what the partitive was doing. \textbf{Du pain} means \emph{an amount of bread} — the article was measuring. A negative says the amount is \textbf{zero}, and there is nothing left to measure, so the measuring article drops out and only the bare \emph{de} remains.

This does \textbf{not} happen to \emph{le}, \emph{la} and \emph{les}. \textbf{Je n'aime pas le café} keeps its article, because that sentence is about coffee in general rather than a quantity of it. So the collapse is a test: if the article was measuring an amount, it goes.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}J'ai du pain.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Je n'ai pas de pain.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Il y a du lait.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Il n'y a pas de lait.\textquotedblright{}
  \item elided — \textquotedblleft{}Je ne bois pas d'eau.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that keeps its article — \textquotedblleft{}Je n'aime pas le café.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the \emph{ne} dropped, as speech does — \textquotedblleft{}Y a pas de pain.\textquotedblright{}
  \item where you are going, and what is not there — \textquotedblleft{}Je vais au café, mais il n'y a pas de café.\textquotedblright{}
  \item about to happen, and refused — \textquotedblleft{}Je vais prendre du pain.\textquotedblright{} / \textquotedblleft{}Je ne vais pas prendre de pain.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do \emph{du}, \emph{de la}, \emph{de l'} and \emph{des} become after a negative? (\textbf{A bare \emph{de}.}) Why? (\textbf{The article was measuring an amount, and the negative makes the amount zero.}) Which articles do \textbf{not} collapse? (\emph{\textbf{Le}}, \emph{\textbf{la}}, \emph{\textbf{les}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Ce qu'on n'entend pas — the chapter, run cold}

\label{lesson:FR-R38-ce-quon-nentend-pas}



\begin{quote}
One rule about sound runs under this whole chapter. State it. Then name the two things that bring a silent consonant back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: silent, and woken}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item silent — \textquotedblleft{}petit, grand, trois, beaucoup\textquotedblright{}
  \item woken by a vowel — \textquotedblleft{}des amis\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}quand est-ce que\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}six ans\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}dix ans\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}neuf ans\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four that sound anyway — \textquotedblleft{}avec, bonjour, neuf, il\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one \emph{t} that refuses — \textquotedblleft{}et un café\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — everything, in the plural and the feminine}
Every noun the book owns, made plural — and listen for how little changes.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the table — \textquotedblleft{}les cafés, les pains, les œufs\textquotedblright{}
  \item the household and the animals — \textquotedblleft{}les frères, les sœurs, les enfants, les chiens, les chats, les amis\textquotedblright{}
  \item the body — \textquotedblleft{}les mains, les têtes, les nez, les bouches\textquotedblright{} — and the one that goes its own way, \textquotedblleft{}l'œil, les yeux\textquotedblright{}
  \item the colours, masculine then feminine — \textquotedblleft{}vert, verte; blanc, blanche; noir, noire; bon, bonne\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ones that never change in the feminine — \textquotedblleft{}rouge, bleu, jaune\textquotedblright{}
  \item the article doing all the work — \textquotedblleft{}le café\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}les cafés\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: and none of it}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four shapes, then their one negative — \textquotedblleft{}du, de la, de l', des\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}pas de\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Il n'y a pas de pain. Il n'y a pas de lait. Il n'y a pas d'eau.\textquotedblright{}
  \item as speech says it — \textquotedblleft{}Y a pas de café.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why is the plural \emph{-s} silent? (\textbf{Because every final consonant is.}) Why is the feminine \emph{-e} audible even though it is silent? (\textbf{It stops the consonant before it being final.}) Why is \emph{chevaux} not irregular? (\textbf{Its \emph{l} became a \emph{u}}.) And what do all four partitives become after a negative? (\textbf{A bare \emph{de}.})
\end{tcolorbox}
